summary: BGP-4 is the path-vector protocol that connects autonomous systems and glues the Internet together. Instead of shortest paths it applies policy: each AS decides which routes to accept, prefer, and advertise.

sections.heading: Autonomous systems and peering
sections.body: An autonomous system (AS) is a set of routers under one administration with a number (ASN). Routers in different ASes peer via eBGP; routers in the same AS exchange routes via iBGP. BGP runs over TCP port 179 (RFC 4271), so it relies on TCP for reliability and has no routing-update retransmission of its own.

sections.heading: Message types
bullets: OPEN: starts a session; carries ASN, hold time, BGP identifier, capabilities.
KEEPALIVE: proves the peer is alive (typically sent at one third of the hold time).
UPDATE: advertises new routes (NLRI + path attributes) or withdraws old ones.
NOTIFICATION: reports an error and closes the session.

sections.heading: Session state machine
sections.body: Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, Established. Routes are exchanged only in Established. A session stuck in Active usually means the TCP connection cannot be made (wrong neighbour address, firewall, or missing route).

sections.heading: Path attributes
bullets: AS_PATH: the list of ASes the route traversed; each AS prepends its own number when advertising to an eBGP peer. Also used for loop prevention: a router rejects a route containing its own ASN.
NEXT_HOP: the address to forward to.
ORIGIN: how the route entered BGP (IGP, EGP, incomplete).
LOCAL_PREF: preference inside an AS; higher is better; not sent to other ASes.
MED: hint to a neighbour AS about the preferred entry point; lower is better.

sections.heading: Best-path selection
sections.body: When several routes to the same prefix exist, BGP picks one in a fixed order (RFC 4271 section 9.1):
bullets: Lowest MED (among routes from the same neighbouring AS).
Lowest IGP cost to the NEXT_HOP.

sections.body: ASes prefer routes from customers (they pay) over peers (settlement-free) over providers (cost money), by setting LOCAL_PREF. They filter exports so they do not give free transit: customer routes go to everyone, peer and provider routes go only to customers.
A router does not re-advertise a route learned from one iBGP peer to another iBGP peer, to avoid loops. So iBGP needs a full mesh, or route reflectors (RFC 4456) or confederations to scale.

A withdrawn route may trigger a sequence of progressively longer alternative paths before settling. Timers such as MRAI (minimum route advertisement interval) and route-flap damping add delay, so global convergence can take minutes.

BGP trusts what neighbours announce. A mistaken or malicious announcement of someone else's prefix can attract traffic. RPKI route-origin validation (ROV) and prefix filtering reduce this; BGPsec adds path validation but is rarely deployed.
Communities (RFC 1997) are 32-bit tags attached to routes, such as 'do not export' or 'set local preference 80', letting neighbours signal policy without per-route configuration.

takeaways: BGP is a path-vector protocol between ASes over TCP port 179.
AS_PATH carries the route history and prevents loops.
Best path: LOCAL_PREF, then shortest AS_PATH, then origin, MED, eBGP over iBGP, IGP cost, router ID.
Policy, not speed, drives BGP; security relies on filtering and RPKI.
